title: The Guru cherishes the Sikh
hookLine: satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal: the True Guru cherishes and protects the Sikh (Sukhmani 18)

lines: STILL RUNNING, A FEW STEPS BEHIND.
cards: A kid learning to ride a bike. The parent runs alongside, one hand on the back of the seat, breathing hard. The kid wobbles, yells don't let go, and the parent says I won't.
Then, at some point, the parent does let go, and keeps running anyway, a few steps behind, just in case. The kid doesn't even know. They think they're doing it alone.
The first stanza of the eighteenth ashtpadi is a list of ways the Guru does exactly this for the Sikh.

teach.b: The stanza opens: satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal. The True Guru cherishes the Sikh. Pratipaal means to nurture, protect, raise up, the way a parent raises a child or a gardener tends a plant.
Then the stanza goes line by line, almost like a list of a parent's jobs.
In paraphrase: the Guru is always kind to the one who serves. The Guru washes away the dirt of the Sikh's bad thinking. The Guru cuts the Sikh's bonds.

The Guru gives the Sikh the wealth of the Name. The Guru sets right the Sikh's life, both this world and the next. And the last line, the tenderest: Nanak, the True Guru holds the Sikh close, like his own life.
Count what's on that list: cleaning, freeing, giving, arranging, holding. In between, the stanza gives the Sikh a part too: the Sikh speaks the Name through the Guru's word, and turns away from vice.
But nowhere does it make the Guru's care wait for the Sikh to ask.

teach.h: CARE THAT RUNS AHEAD OF THE ASK.
teach.b: That's the feel of pratipaal: care that runs ahead of the request. And it's ongoing: not a single rescue, but a whole relationship.

teach.h: THE HYMN, THE SANGAT, THE PLATE.
teach.b: Sikhs today speak of meeting that care through the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat: a hymn that lands on the right day, a langar plate handed over before anyone asked.
Some would say they've been held like the kid on the bike more often than they noticed. Today's word is an invitation to look for it. Not to earn.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the eighteenth ashtpadi's first stanza on how the True Guru cherishes the Sikh, and Sikhs speak of meeting that care through the Guru Granth Sahib and the sangat.

o: to test a learner before giving a lesson
to nurture, protect and raise up, like a parent
to punish a student who breaks the rules

games.q: the Guru cherishes the Sikh — tap the pairs.

s: the stanza describes the Guru's care as a single rescue
it's an ongoing relationship: cleaning, freeing, giving, holding.
pratipaal is the kind of care a parent or gardener gives
to nurture, protect and raise up.
the stanza's lines are only about what the Guru does
it alternates: the Guru cleans and frees; the Sikh speaks the Name and turns from vice.

games.q: you're the kid on the bike and you think you're riding alone. by the eighteenth ashtpadi's first stanza, what's true?
o: you're being held more than you notice.
you'd better ask for help first.
games.why: the stanza lists care that runs ahead of the ask, ending: the True Guru holds the Sikh close, like his own life.

practice: Let yourself be supported by the chair, the floor, the air you're breathing.
Then think back to one time you were cared for before you asked, a meal left out for you, a ride offered, a word at the right time, and let yourself feel it again without explaining it away.
If you pray, you can feel that care as the Guru's; if not, just let it be care.

wordCard.voice: Pratipaal, to nurture, protect, raise up. Satgur sikh kee karai pratipaal: care that cleans, frees, gives and holds the Sikh close, like the Guru's own life.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pratipaal, nurturing, protecting, raising up.

carryVoice: Your line: cherished. Care that runs ahead of the asking is still care, noticed or not. Day five hundred seven.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 18, stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286)
